items.title: Light makes the inside of a chloroplast 1000 times more acidic
items.claim: In dark chloroplasts, stroma and thylakoid lumen are both about pH 7. Turn on the light: protons are pumped from stroma INTO thylakoid lumen. Lumen pH drops to ~5; stroma rises to ~8. That's a thousand-fold proton concentration difference.

options.text: The proton gradient drives ATP synthase: protons flow back through the enzyme from lumen to stroma, powering ATP synthesis. The light reactions store light energy as a transmembrane proton gradient, just as respiration does

items.reveal:
Light reactions in chloroplast thylakoid membranes:
1. Photosystem II uses light to oxidise water (releasing O2) and reduce plastoquinone. Protons are released INSIDE the lumen.
2. Cytochrome b6f passes electrons on while also pumping protons FROM stroma TO lumen.
3. Photosystem I uses light to push electrons to NADP+, making NADPH (in the stroma).
4. Net result: lumen accumulates protons, stroma loses them. pH gradient ~3 units (1000x concentration).

ATP synthase (CF1-CF0) in the thylakoid membrane lets protons flow back from lumen to stroma. The enzyme rotates, synthesises ATP from ADP and Pi. ATP and NADPH are released INTO the stroma, where the Calvin cycle uses them to fix CO2.

This is exactly analogous to mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Same chemistry, opposite source — solar input rather than food oxidation. Both use the proton motive force to make ATP.

The parallel was predicted by Peter Mitchell in 1961 and confirmed experimentally over the next two decades.
items.why: Photosynthesis is taught as if it makes sugar directly from light. Light first powers a proton pump; the pump powers ATP synthesis; ATP plus NADPH then power sugar synthesis. Energy storage is layered.

items.title: About 90% of your serotonin is made in your gut
items.claim: Serotonin is famous as a mood-related brain chemical. But ~90% of the body's serotonin is in the gut, where it regulates gut motility and is influenced by gut bacteria. The gut and brain communicate via the vagus nerve and circulating molecules.

options.text: A direct neural connection like an optic nerve

A multi-channel system: vagus nerve sends ~80% afferent (gut-to-brain) signals; immune signalling; circulating short-chain fatty acids and neurotransmitters from gut bacteria — all influence brain function bidirectionally
A myth — the gut and brain don't talk

items.reveal_title: The enteric nervous system and microbial signals
items.reveal:
The gut has its own nervous system (the enteric nervous system, ENS) with ~500 million neurons — about as many as a cat's brain. The ENS controls gut motility, secretion and absorption largely independently of the central nervous system.

The vagus nerve connects gut and brain. About 80% of vagus fibres are afferent (carrying signals FROM gut TO brain). Gut chemical and stretch receptors continuously inform the brain about digestive state.

Serotonin: ~90% is in enterochromaffin cells of the gut, regulating peristalsis and pain signalling. Drugs targeting gut serotonin (e.g., 5-HT3 antagonists) treat IBS and chemotherapy nausea.

Gut bacteria contribute by:
- Producing short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, propionate) from fibre, which affect blood-brain barrier permeability and microglial function.
- Producing or modulating neurotransmitters (GABA, serotonin precursors).
- Influencing tryptophan metabolism (the precursor for serotonin).
- Modulating systemic inflammation.

Germ-free mice (raised without bacteria) show altered behaviour, anxiety, and brain development — restored by giving them normal gut bacteria. Effects in humans are more modest but real (e.g., faecal microbiota transplants can influence mood markers in some patients).

The gut-brain field is young and much remains speculative. Causal direction and effect sizes in humans are still being mapped.
items.why: Brain chemistry feels like brain-only territory. Much of our serotonin is in the gut; bacteria influence brain function via multiple routes. The body's signalling architecture is broader than its anatomy suggests.
